¶
'''wizen-faced''' (wiz′n-fāst), ''a.'' Having a thin, shriveled face.
{{smaller block|The story is connected with a dingy ''wizen-faced'' portrait in an oval frame. {{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 50.}}
The door . . . was slowly opened, and a little blear-eyed, ''weazen-faced'' ancient man came creeping out. {{right|''Dickens'', Martin Chuzzlewit, xi.}}}}

'''wizier''', ''n.'' Same as ''vizir.''

'''wizzen†''', ''a.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''wizen.''

'''wk.''' A contraction of ''week.''

'''wlappe†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''wlappen'', var. of ''wrappen'': see ''wrap'' and ''lap''<sup>2</sup>.] To wrap; roll up.
{{smaller block|ȝe schulen fynde a ȝong child ''wlappid'' in clothis, and put in a cracche. {{right|''Wyclif'', Luke ii. 12.}}}}

'''wlate†''', ''v. i.'' and ''t.'' [ME. ''wlaten'', < AS. ''wlǣtian'', loathe.] To feel disgust; loathe; abominate.
{{smaller block|<poem>So the worcher of this worlde ''wlates'' ther-wyth
That in the poynt of her play he poruayes a mynde.</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 1501.}}}}

'''wlatsome†, wlatsom†''', ''a.'' [< ME. ''wlatsom'', ''wlatsum'', loathsome, abominable, < *''wlate'' (< AS. ''wlætte''), nausea, disgust, + ''-som'', E. ''-some.''] Loathsome; detestable; hateful.
{{smaller block|<poem>For thouȝ the soule haue thi lijknes,
Man is but ''wlatsum'' erthe and clay.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 173.}}
<poem>Mordre is so ''wlatsom'' and abhominable
To God, that is so just and resonable,
That he ne wol nat suffre it heled be.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 233.}}}}

''vizkr'', clever, knowing, sagacious, for *''vitskr'', < ''vita'', know: see ''wit''1. Cf. ''witch''1, ult. from the same root, but having no immediate connection with ''wizard''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1†.''' A wise man; a sage. {{smaller block|Hee that cannot personate the wise-man well among ''wizards'', let him learne to play the foole well amongst dizzards. {{right|''Chapman'', Masque of Middle Temple and Lincoln’s Inn.}}}} {{smaller block|See how from far, upon the eastern road, The star-led ''wizards'' haste with odours sweet. {{right|''Milton'', Nativity, l. 23.}}}} '''2.''' A proficient in the occult sciences; an adept in the black art; one supposed to possess supernatural powers, generally from having leagued himself with the Evil One; a sorcerer; an enchanter; a magician; hence, a title occasionally applied to, or assumed by, modern performers of legerdemain; a conjurer; a juggler. See ''witch''1. {{smaller block|And the soul that turneth after such as have familiar spirits, and after ''wizards'', . . . I will even set my face against that soul. {{right|Lev. xx. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|If by any Accident they do hear of the Thief, all is ascrib’d to the wonderful Cunning of their ''Wissard''. {{right|Quoted in ''Ashton’s'' Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne,}} {{right|[I. 121.}}}} {{smaller block|No ''wizards'' now ply their trade of selling favorable winds to the Norwegian coasters. {{right|''B. Taylor'', Northern Travel, p. 136.}}}} '''II.''' ''a.'' Magic; having magical powers; enchanting: as, a ''wizard'' spell. {{smaller block|Where Deva spreads her ''wizard'' stream. {{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 55.}}}} '''wizardly''' (wiz′ärd-li), ''adv.''   [< ''wizard'' + ''-ly''1.]   Resembling a wizard; characteristic of a wizard. [Rare.] '''wizardry''' (wiz′ärd-ri), ''n.''   [< ''wizard'' + ''-ry''.]   The art or practices of wizards; sorcery. {{smaller block|''Wizardry'' and dealing with evil spirits. {{right|''Milman'', Latin Christianity, xi. 9.}}}} '''wize†.''' Hence ''wizen''1, ''v.'']   Hard, dry, and shriveled; withered. {{smaller block|A gay little ''wizen'' old man, in appearance, from the Eastern climate’s dilapidations upon his youth and health. {{right|''Mme. ''wā'', interj., sometimes used with dat. case, also in combination ''wā lā'', ''wā lā wā'', also ''wālā wā'', alas! lit. woe! lo! woe! (> ult. E. ''wellaway'', ''welladay'') = D. ''wee'' = LG. ''wee'' = G. ''weh'' = Icel. ''vei'' = Sw. ''ve'' = Dan. ''vee'' = Goth. ''wai'', interj., woe! (cf. OF. ''ouais'' = It. Sp. ''guai'', woe! < Teut.) = L. ''væ'', woe! (''væ victis'', woe to the vanquished!) = Gr. οἴ! οὐαί! woe! ah! oh! an exclamation of pain, etc., out of which the other uses grew. Hence ult. ''woe'', ''n.'', ''wail''1, and ''wellaway'', ''welladay''; cf. also ''waiment.'']   Alas! an exclamation of pain or grief. See ''woe'', ''n.'' {{smaller block|Alas and ''woe!'' {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 14. 107.}}}} '''woe''' (wō), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Also ''wo''; Sc. ''wae''; < ME. ''wo'', ''woo'', ''wa'', also ''wee'', the last from AS. ''weá'', pl. ''weán'', a form not immediately derivable from the interj. ''wā'', but standing for *''wǣ'' (*''wǣw-'') = OS. ''wē'' (''wēw-'') = D. ''wee'' = LG. ''wee'' = OHG. MHG. ''wē'' (''wēw-''), OHG. also ''wēwo'', m., ''wēwa'', f., G. ''wehe'' = Dan. ''vee'', woe, = Goth. *''wai'' (> It. ''guajo'', pain); prob. from the interj.: see ''woe'', ''interj.'']   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' Grief; sorrow; misery; heavy calamity. {{smaller block|They, outcast from God, are here condemn’d To waste eternal days in ''woe'' and pain.{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 695.}}}} '''2.''' A heavy calamity; an affliction. {{smaller block|One ''woe'' is past; and, behold, there come two ''woes'' more hereafter. {{right|Rev. ix. 12.}}}} {{smaller block|''Woe'' is frequently used in denunciations, either with the optative mood of the verb or alone, and thus in an interjectional manner (see ''woe'', ''interj.'').}} {{smaller block|''Woe be'' unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep! {{right|Jer. xxiii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|''Woe'' to the vanquished, ''woe!'' {{right|''Dryden'', Albion and Albanius, i. 1.}}}} ''Woe'' to the dupe, and ''woe'' to the deceiver! ''Woe'' to the oppressed, and ''woe'' to the oppressor! {{smaller block|{{right|''Shelley'', Hellas.}}}} {{smaller|It is also used in exclamations of sorrow, in such cases the noun or pronoun following being really in the dative.}} {{smaller block|''Woe'' is me! for I am undone. {{right|Isa. vi. 5.}}}} {{smaller block|''Woe'' was the knight at this severe command. {{right|''Dryden'', Wife of Bath, l. 108.}}}} {{smaller block|An’ aye the o’ercome o’ his sang Was “''Wae'' ’s me for Prince Charlie!” {{right|''W. Glen'', A Wee Bird cam’ to our Ha’ Door.}}}} {{smaller|'''In weal and woe''', in prosperity and adversity. ''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 987.—'''Woe worth the day.''' See ''worth''1, 3.='''Syn.''' Distress, tribulation, affliction, bitterness, unhappiness, wretchedness. ''Woe'' is an intense unhappiness; the word is strong and elevated, almost poetical.}} '''II.'''† ''a.'' Sad; sorrowful; miserable; woeful; wretched. {{smaller block|Ofte hadde Horn beo ''wo'' Ac neure wurs than him was tho. {{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|In this debat I was so ''wo'', Me thoghte myn herte braste atweyn. {{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 1192.}}}} {{smaller block|He was full ''wo'', and gan his former griefe renew. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. i. 38.}}}} {{smaller block|Childe Waters was a ''woe'' man, good Lord, To see faire Ellen swimme! {{right|''Child Waters'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 208).}}}} '''woebegone, wobegone''' (wō′bẹ̄-gôn″), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. ''woe-begon''; < ME. ''wo-begon'', ''wo-bygon''; < ''woe'', ''wo'', ''n.'', woe, sorrow, + ''begone''1.]   Overwhelmed with woe; immersed in grief or sorrow; also, sorrowful; rueful; indicating woe or distress: as, a ''woebegone'' look. {{smaller block|Thow farest ek by me, thow Pandarus! As he that, whan a wight is ''wo-bygon'', He cometh to him apaas, and seith right thus: “Thynke nat on smerte and thow shalt fele none!” {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 464.}}}} {{smaller block|Coumfort hem that careful been, And helpe hem that ben ''woo bigoon.'' {{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 16.}}}} {{smaller block|Even such a man, so faint, so spiritless, So dull, so dead in look, so ''woe-begone'', Drew Priam’s curtain in the dead of night. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 1. 71.}}}} {{smaller block|Each man looked ruefully in his neighbor’s face in search of encouragement, but only found in its ''woe-begone'' lineaments a confirmation of his own dismay. {{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 438.}}}} {{smaller|In early use the two words are sometimes separated.}} {{smaller block|''Wo'' was this wrecched woman tho ''bigoon.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 820.}}}} '''woeful, woful''' (wō′fu̇l), ''a.''   [Sc. ''waeful''; < ME. ''woful, wofull''; < ''woe'' + ''-ful.'']   '''1.''' Full of woe; distressed with grief or calamity; afflicted; sorrowful. {{smaller block|O verrey goost, that errest to and fro! Whi niltow flen out of the ''wofulleste'' Body that evere myght on grounde go? {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 303.}}}} {{smaller block|What now willt thou don, ''woful'' Eglentine? To gret heuynesse off-fors moste thou incline. {{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2163.}}}} {{smaller block|Weep no more, ''woful'' shepherds. {{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 165.}}}}
